pageCache.text:
Welcome toRushcombe First School
Rushcombe is a friendly and caring school for children aged four to nine years old. Children’s early experiences lay the foundations for the rest of their lives and we are committed to providing high quality education for all children in partnership with parents. We provide an exciting and innovative curriculum within a safe, stimulating and caring environment where children are welcomed as individuals, where they can be confident, secure and are valued for all they achieve.
As a large first school with high standards of achievement, our experienced and dedicated team of teaching and support staff get to know each child and work with you in helping your child to succeed. We encourage the children to demonstrate independence, involvement and responsibility in and for their learning, with the highest standards of effort and behaviour. We believe that the children of Rushcombe will be inspired and fulfilled, and will become responsible and confident members of the community with a lifelong enthusiasm for learning.
This website will provide a range of information about our school, however, you are welcome to visit us to find out more. I would be happy to meet you and discuss the school in more detail and answer any questions you may have. On your visit you will see our attractive and well-equipped school and grounds, meet some of our children and observe their learning and achievements. I look forward to meeting you, and your child, and welcoming you to our school.
Yours sincerely, Caroline Mahon, Headteacher

Home and School Partnership
The child’s first and most significant educators are the child’s parents / carers. From the moment the child is born (or even before), the nature of the experiences and dialogue within the home environment, contribute significantly to the development of the child. When the child starts school, they have the opportunity to engage in a range of experiences to develop their academic, personal and social skills, building upon and extending the experiences developed in the home. As a result, it is important that families and school see the child’s education and development as a shared responsibility, recognising the unique experiences that each can bring.
Positive relationships between home and school are crucial. It is important to show the child that home and school are places that work together, with the child’s best interests at the centre of everything we do. In addition to termly parent consultation evenings, parents are always welcome to discuss their child’s development and progress by arranging to talk with their child’s class teacher. We also look forward to welcoming you to the variety of school events that take place throughout the school year.
By forging a mutually respectful home and school partnership, we enhance the opportunities for the child to flourish and to realise their full potential.

pageCache.pageTitle: The Creative Arts | Rushcombe First School Hanham Road,  Corfe Mullen, Wimborne, Dorset BH21 3PX
pageCache.text:
The Creative Arts
The creative arts are an important part of the Rushcombe curriculum because we believe that the opportunity to develop self-expression is a fundamental part of human experience.
Within each of our Learning Adventures, we aim to provide opportunities for children to express themselves through the arts – whether that’s through drawing, painting, sculpture, music, dance, drama or any other form of expression. Children develop skills, explore ideas, create their own art works and engage in reflection and evaluation of what they have produced. The school’s Learning Adventures provide a range of purposeful contexts for learning in the arts to take place.
The school’s approach to the arts is informed by the Reggio Emilia schools in Italy, where the child is conceptualised as an artist in their own right and is supported to develop their own art projects and expressions through co-constructive approaches. The founder of the Reggio Emilia schools, Loris Malaguzi believed that children have a multitude of ways in which they can express themselves and he encapsulated this belief within his poem ‘The Hundred Languages of Children’. At Rushcombe First School, we also believe passionately that children have many ways in which they can express themselves, (sometimes combining multiple forms of communication and media) and that we have a duty to enable them to explore these means of expression. This belief runs through our delivery of the creative arts, and is also central to our yearly Reggio inspired projects, in which children participate in studio work to develop individual or group expressions.
In addition, regular opportunities are provided for children to learn from a range of arts professionals, including practising artists, dancers, musicians, actors and drama facilitators (see Theatre in Education for further details). We believe that these opportunities play a valuable role in enriching the child’s experiences and enabling them to explore their creativity. We have worked with many wonderful artists over recent years to develop some truly spectacular projects. These have included our whole school puppet shows (developed with Creation Myth Puppets), in which all children in the school participate. As part of these projects, the children work with an artist to write and create a story and then make the puppets with which they perform. The result is a wonderful performance developed by all of the children, incorporating an important message about our world. Other arts projects have included working with an artist to create a large scale, interactive installation of an imagined island in the school hall and creating an outside, night time illuminated performance entitled ‘Delights of the Deep’ (in conjunction with the artist Sarah Butterworth). We believe that the arts are a vital part of human experience and therefore they are a vital part of the life of our school.

pageCache.pageTitle: Personal and Social Development | Rushcombe First School Hanham Road,  Corfe Mullen, Wimborne, Dorset BH21 3PX
pageCache.text:
Personal and Social Development
As a school, we recognise the importance of supporting the development of the whole child. Alongside the child’s academic development, the nurturing of their personal and social skills are crucial aspects of the child’s learning. We aim to support children to become confident individuals, who are aware of their emotions and recognise their own self-worth, whilst building positive relationships and friendships. Emotional health and well-being are supported through a combination of the school’s ethos, curriculum and teaching approaches, which seek to nurture children as individuals and to develop their self-esteem.
Across the academic year, children engage with a range of learning themes to support their personal and social development. These aspects are delivered through the PSHE (Personal, Social and Health Education) curriculum. The themes that children explore include learning how to stay safe online, learning that their body belongs to them through the ‘pants are private’ programme (NSPCC), exploring how to recognise and deal with bullying, developing positive friendships and relationships, learning about emotions, and how to be mentally and physically healthy. A key aspect of the PSHE curriculum also involves enabling children to develop a respect for differences and for their own uniqueness. Children explore the importance of respecting differences based upon the things we like to do, cultural heritage, or where we come from in the world. They learn about gender stereotypes, develop their understanding of disability, and explore the importance of respecting physical differences, including the colour of our skin. In addition, they learn that there are many different types of family. By engaging with these different themes, we aim for all children to develop respect for themselves and for the diverse world they are entering into.

Extra-Curricular Activities
The school offers a broad range of extra-curricular activities, which aim to enrich the children’s learning experiences. Extra-curricular clubs provide the opportunity for children to develop skills and foster their enjoyment across a range of areas.
Clubs are generally offered on a termly basis, so that children have the opportunity to try different activities and pursue a range of interests across the year. There are some clubs that are ongoing throughout the school year, such as football or singing, enabling children to build their skills and develop their interests across the longer term.
Clubs on offer typically include a range of sports and creative arts (art and design, dance, drama and music) across the academic year. In addition, there will be other options, which could include computing, cookery, French, gardening, mindfulness and nature club (to name but a few).

pageCache.text:
Cultural Learning & RE
As a school, we aim to ensure that our children are equipped with the attitudes and understanding that will enable them to make a positive contribution to the world they are entering into. Being able to understand and respect differences between people, cultures and beliefs is an important attribute to instil within children for the future. Alongside this, we aim for children to recognise the needs, rights and responsibilities that we all share.
The school’s curriculum provides a range of opportunities for children to learn about different cultures and beliefs. Through their cultural learning, children explore a range of artistic traditions (Art and Design) and learn about the experiences of people in different communities around the world (Geography), making comparisons with their own lives, communities and experiences. Our Religious Education curriculum (informed by the Dorset SACRE Agreed Syllabus for Religious Education) provides the opportunity for children to learn about a range of world beliefs and to gain their own personal insights into what it means to live within a multi faith society, and to reflect upon what it means to be human. Within every year group, children carry out a focused study of Christianity and a focused study of another world religion. Each year group also carries out a thematic study, which aims to provide opportunities for children to make comparisons between different religions, recognising the many common values that exist between the belief systems they study. We supplement this learning through the use of philosophy sessions, which aim to develop children’s positive attitudes towards valuing the ideas and contributions that others bring. In addition, once children enter key stage 2, they begin to learn a modern foreign language (French), which further supports their respect for our diverse world, whilst also developing their communication skills.

pageCache.text:
Early Years
The school’s early years foundation stage is a time when children are nurtured into our school community, laying the foundations for their time at the school and for their future learning. Working closely with families and preschools, we aim to provide a smooth transition for your child’s start at school, helping them to settle quickly and enjoy the new and exciting opportunities they will experience. Building relationships and developing confidence are key aspects at this stage, enabling your child to develop friendships, build bonds with their teachers and to feel valued as individuals. Children will benefit from a large, open plan classroom environment, supplemented by our early years outdoor area, both of which are designed along Reggio Emilia principles to encourage interactions and explorations. Children’s learning experiences are developed in line with the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS), focused upon the seven key areas of learning:
Learning is developed within these areas through a balance of child-initiated experiences (TED) and through direct teaching where appropriate, for example, regular phonics sessions. Children’s writing skills and mathematical development are supported within small groups, enabling focused guidance and support from the teacher. Children in foundation take part in the school’s Learning Adventures from the very beginning of their time at the school, and as the year progresses, there will be opportunities for them to collaborate on projects with children from other year groups and to take part in the rich variety of school events that take place. Through our nurturing and relationship focused approach, we aim to make this important year a time of wonder and discovery for all children.

pageCache.pageTitle: English | Rushcombe First School Hanham Road,  Corfe Mullen, Wimborne, Dorset BH21 3PX
pageCache.text:
English
Developing key English skills is a central part of the school’s curriculum. The English curriculum includes reading, writing and spoken language.
Children’s reading skills are initially developed through a focus upon phonetic development. Regular reading, both in school and at home help to develop children’s skills and confidence. Developing the child’s comprehension skills begins early, with adult questioning enabling children to think about the meaning of what is being read. As children become increasingly confident and independent readers, they will be exposed to more challenging texts and will be supported to develop their ability to answer more complex questions about what they are reading.
Children’s writing skills are developed through a range of engaging contexts for writing linked to our Learning Adventure themes. Children explore the features of a range of text types, including story writing, poetry, play scripts, non-fiction reports, recounts and persuasive writing. They develop their grammar, punctuation and spelling skills through focused taught sessions, enabling them to develop the quality of their writing. This is accompanied by regular handwriting practice.
Spoken language involves children developing their competencies of engaging in dialogue in a range of contexts. They are provided with opportunities to explore and develop their spoken language skills in a range of ways, including through paired / small group work, presenting ideas to the class and engaging in Philosophical discussion.
The school delivers the National Curriculum programmes of study for English. These programmes of study can be found online by clicking here

pageCache.pageTitle: Humanities | Rushcombe First School Hanham Road,  Corfe Mullen, Wimborne, Dorset BH21 3PX
pageCache.text:
Humanities
The humanities areas of History and Geography are an integral part of the Rushcombe curriculum. Each academic year, the school develops a bespoke Learning Adventure with a focus upon history, and another with a focus upon geography, both delivered through the school’s mantle of the expert approach. Historical and geographical content is also reinforced at appropriate points within other Learning Adventures, so that knowledge and understanding is consolidated within long term memory.
At Rushcombe First School, we aim to provide an approach to the history curriculum, which is based upon research into the most effective approaches to historical learning. The school provides specialist teaching in ancient history, providing children with an understanding of the development of human civilisation from its earliest beginnings, including explorations of the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages, supplemented by comparative studies with other periods from ancient history, including Ancient Greece, the Ancient Egyptians, the Romans, the Anglo-Saxons and Vikings. The school has developed an innovative and highly engaging approach to the teaching of ancient history, utilising external expertise, the school’s extensive grounds and experiential learning. Through this approach, historical learning is stimulated by the development of historical settlements (spanning from the Stone Age to the Iron Age) on the school grounds, which children can explore in a variety of ways through our Mantle of the Expert approach. Our history curriculum aims to develop children’s love of history, laying the foundations for them to become the historians, archaeologists and anthropolgists of the future.
The geography curriculum at Rushcombe First School aims to provide children with a sense of awe and wonder about the world that we live in, recognising that our world is a place full of human and physical diversity, whilst also exploring some of the challenges and inequalities that are brought into focus through geographical study. By delivering the geography curriculum through a mantle of the expert approach, children’s geographical learning is placed within highly motivating and meaningful contexts, for example, by imagining they are going on an expedition to South America, or by setting up their own travel agency. Through this approach, children are supported to develop their geographical knowledge, understanding and skills, including their locational and place knowledge, making comparisons between different regions, developing their understanding of human and physical features, using maps and carrying out fieldwork.

pageCache.pageTitle: Learning Adventures | Rushcombe First School Hanham Road,  Corfe Mullen, Wimborne, Dorset BH21 3PX
pageCache.text:
Learning Adventures
The school’s curriculum is delivered through our ‘Learning Adventures’, which provide an engaging and purposeful theme for the children’s learning. The children will explore a new Learning Adventure every half term, with a balance of curriculum areas being explored across the academic year. Through our Learning Adventures, we cover many aspects of the early years curriculum (Foundation) and the National Curriculum (Years 1-4).
Learning Adventure themes are the same for all year groups across the school, but the content will be adapted to meet the key learning objectives for each specific year group. By using a single theme across the school, we build our whole school learning community, enabling children from different year groups to come together to share their learning experiences.
Each of the school’s Learning Adventures begins with an engaging starting point, which aims to foster children’s curiosity and interest in the theme to be explored – this may take the form of a special event or a thought provoking scenario for the children to experience. As a Learning Adventure develops, the teachers aim to construct the learning with the children, incorporating the children’s ideas and questions as they emerge. Towards the end of each Learning Adventure, there is also a special ‘finale’ event, in which children have the opportunity to showcase and celebrate the learning that has taken place.
When delivering our Learning Adventures, the school often works with a range of external artists, experts and drama facilitators to help bring the learning to life for the children and to further enrich their experiences. Each Learning Adventure is entirely bespoke to the school, often taking the form of a unique creative project and utilising actors and artists in residence for extended periods of time.

pageCache.pageTitle: Mantle of the Expert | Rushcombe First School Hanham Road,  Corfe Mullen, Wimborne, Dorset BH21 3PX
pageCache.text:
Mantle of the Expert
Mantle of the Expert is an approach to teaching that is used across the school. The approach is a dramatic-inquiry based approach to teaching and learning, which was developed by Professor Dorothy Heathcote in the 1980s.
Mantle of the Expert involves the children carrying out their learning from the perspective of an expert, for example, this could be as an archaeologist, engineer, royal advisor or geologist. By placing the child within the role of an expert, we aim to fully immerse children within the learning experience and to empower them to make decisions about the direction that their learning may take.
Whenever the Mantle of the Expert approach is utilised within the classroom, an ‘enterprise’ will be set for the children to complete. The enterprise is the overarching ‘big task’ that children will be working towards in their role as an expert, for example, as engineers they may be asked to build a car to break the land speed record. When working towards this enterprise, the children will need to consider the tasks that need to be completed in order to work towards this aim – in this example they may decide that they need to start by carrying out scientific testing about what might affect the speed of a car.
When utilising the Mantle of the Expert approach, teachers work alongside the children to break the enterprise into smaller tasks. Teachers utilise their professional expertise to incorporate key curriculum objectives within the emerging classroom projects. In the above example, a decision to explore what makes a car go fast, can lead into an opportunity for a focused scientific investigation into the effects of friction. By utilising this approach, the different aspects of the curriculum can be explored in a highly purposeful way that has relevance to the children’s experiences.
In addition to the children going into role as experts, a key part of the approach often involves the teachers going into the role of a ‘client’ – the client is the person or representative that needs the enterprise to be completed. By going into role as a range of characters, the teacher is able to deliver a range of problems or tasks to the group in a highly engaging way – they are able to bring the character back to the class at different points to check on progress and to introduce new dilemmas for the children to think about.

pageCache.text:
Mathematics
Enabling children to become numerate, confident mathematicians is a key aim of the school’s curriculum. During their time at Rushcombe, children will develop their understanding across a range of mathematical areas, including the number system, calculating, fractions and decimals, measures, shape and space and geometry.
Children develop their conceptual understanding by revisiting key concepts regularly and by exploring a range of practical resources and pictorial representations, before moving on to more abstract ways of recording. The emphasis is placed upon exploring concepts in a range of ways, so that secure conceptual understanding can be developed.
Mental skills, written strategies, problem solving and mathematical reasoning are also key aspects of the children’s learning in Maths. Children develop their mental skills across a range of areas, including learning their number bonds, mental addition / subtraction skills and times tables and division facts. Children also develop a range of written calculation strategies, including the use of formal written methods.
Regular opportunities are provided for children to engage in mathematical problem solving and investigations, including applying their skills in real life contexts. Children are supported to understand what different problems require them to do and are encouraged to reflect upon their strategies and to make changes where required. Children also explore and discuss their mathematical reasoning linked to a range of concepts.
The school delivers the National Curriculum programmes of study for Mathematics. These programmes of study can be found online by clicking here

pageCache.text:
Reggio Approaches
Rushcombe First School’s ethos and approaches are influenced by the world-renowned Reggio Emilia schools in northern Italy, which base their philosophy of education upon the belief in an empowered, competent child. Within the Reggio schools, childhood is respected and nurtured, children’s rights are central to the ethos that is developed, and children are valued as contributors to society. One of the key beliefs of the Reggio Approach is the view of the child as a co-creator of the learning that takes place. As a result, there is an emphasis upon the child as a curious individual who constructs their knowledge and understanding of the world, alongside the skilful support and facilitation of the teacher. Children are viewed as capable of expressing themselves in a multitude of ways and are seen as artists, bringing their own valuable insights to the world. The child’s voice is central to the daily life of the Reggio schools, nurtured through an emphasis upon the fostering of interactions and communications between all participants.
At Rushcombe First School, we apply Reggio inspired approaches in a range of ways:
The school is proud to be one of the few schools nationally that embeds these principles within our ethos and approaches to learning. We believe that by placing these approaches at the centre of our ethos, we contribute to respecting and empowering childhood within modern day society. Research Basis
At Rushcombe First School, we aim to provide each child with the very best educational start in life, equipping them with the skills they need to thrive in the future. In order to do this, we believe it is important that we understand and utilise the most effective teaching approaches to enable our young learners to achieve their potential. The approaches that we utilise at Rushcombe First School are based upon extensive research about how children learn and develop.
The Rushcombe learning ethos is based upon a firm belief that learning happens best when it happens with the child. Traditional models of education from the Victorian times often viewed learning as something which happened to the child, for example, it was seen as a one-way process involving the teacher giving knowledge to a passive recipient child. Our belief as a school however is that the child is the central aspect of the learning process, whose ideas, curiosity, self-awareness and individual responsibility are the starting point for all learning that takes place, and which the teacher has the responsibility to respect and build upon.
The Rushcombe approach builds upon extensive research into the theories of educational theorists and psychologists such as Jean Piaget, Jerome Bruner and Lev Vygotsky – all of whose theories are commonly viewed as belonging to a ‘constructivist’ school of thought. The work of Jean Piaget viewed the child as playing an active role in their own learning, emphasising the importance of the child’s explorations, observations and experimentations. Lev Vygotsky’s work focused upon the importance of social interactions within the learning process, exploring how adults help children to move forward with their learning, whilst retaining the child’s own active participation. Meanwhile, Jerome Bruner completed work on the self-awareness of the learner (or ‘learning how to learn’) and carried out significant work into designing effective curricula to enable children to understand complex information. Although each theorist brings different perspectives, they share the commonality that learning should be ‘constructed with the learner’.
Our research into the constructivist theorists has led to us developing a range of strategies to ensure that co-construction between the child and teacher is at the centre of everything we do. High quality discussion, questioning and dialogue is at the heart of interactions between the teacher and the child, helping children to articulate their ideas and thinking. In addition to this, we utilise teaching approaches such as Mantle of the Expert, Philosophy sessions, Reggio approaches and TED which provide scope for children to share their ideas and make decisions about the direction of a particular episode of learning. Embedded within this approach is how teachers look to incorporate children’s emerging ideas and interests within their planning. In addition, each of our taught sessions begins with an exploration phase, which provides children with the opportunity to raise questions and make discoveries as a starting point for their learning. As a result, the child’s voice and perspective within the learning process is fostered, with the teacher utilising their professional expertise to help guide the learning forward.
These approaches are also supplemented by research into other areas of good practice, including the work of Dylan William on the use of assessment, Barack Rosenshine’s work on the principles of effective instruction, a range of research into the role of memory in learning, and other research based findings from the Education Endowment Foundation. By incorporating this range of research-based practices, we aim to provide the very best educational experiences for the children at Rushcombe First School.

Science and Technology
The STEM subjects of science, design technology and computing are a central part of the school’s curriculum, enabling children to develop their skills and understanding within these areas, whilst also developing links between them. Alongside regular opportunities to develop computing and scientific investigation skills across the year, the school also delivers an annual Learning Adventure in which the STEM subjects are the primary focus. Our STEM focused Learning Adventures are delivered through a mantle of the expert approach, providing highly motivating and purposeful contexts for the children’s learning in these areas. As a result of this high-quality provision, we aim to develop children’s love of the STEM subjects, whilst also developing the scientists, engineers and technology specialists of the future.
ScienceThe Rushcombe science curriculum aims to empower each child to view themselves as scientists, capable of making their own discoveries about the world around them. Each academic year, the school develops a Learning Adventure which provides a focus upon environmental science, including the study of living things and habitats. In addition, our STEM themed Learning Adventures provide opportunities for scientific study linked to everyday materials (key stage 1) and physics (key stage 2). Our approach to learning in science couples regular scientific inquiry with the development of scientific knowledge, and covers a range of areas based upon the programmes of study from the National Curriculum. Children are regularly encouraged to raise their own scientific questions and to plan their own investigations, before engaging in careful analysis of results and drawing conclusions.
Design TechnologyThe Rushcombe design technology curriculum provides a range of highly engaging product design and make projects. Children develop their Design Technology skills by analysing products in the environment around them, developing their own designs, practising skills, creating prototypes, developing final products and engaging in testing and evaluation. During their time at Rushcombe First School, children explore aspects such as designing and making freestanding structures, making moving vehicles / toys and products controlled by computer programming.
ComputingThe computing curriculum is delivered across the academic year, with children regularly developing and practising their skills within a range of curriculum areas and Learning Adventures. Taught lessons focus specifically upon skills development and are supplemented by regular opportunities to apply and develop skills in creative, purposeful contexts. The foundation of the computing curriculum supports children to use technology safely and responsibly, particularly when working online. During their time at the school, children develop a broad range of knowledge and skills, including developing their understanding of the internet, using a variety of software to accomplish certain goals and designing, writing and debugging programs.

TED (Time to Explore and Discover)
TED is a key part of the Rushcombe curriculum – it stands for Time to Explore and Discover. Children in Foundation will engage in daily TED sessions (reinforcing the child-initiated aspects of the early years curriculum), whereas older children may participate in TED projects that run over a block of consecutive days.
During TED time, children engage in self-directed tasks – they plan what they would like to do, carry out investigations and projects, and make their own learning discoveries. During this time, the teachers will work alongside your child, engaging in discussion with them and asking questions to support their thinking and to help extend their tasks in productive ways. Children are encouraged to evaluate what they are doing and to review their learning upon completion, possibly finding new ideas for next steps. Engaging in TED supports the development of the child as a motivated, curious learner, including enhancing self-awareness and their Learning Hero skills (for example, making changes to their project work, just like Adaptable Armadillo). TED sessions also provide opportunities for children to practise and apply a range of skills from other curriculum areas.

Theatre in Education
Closely linked to our Mantle of the Expert approach, is the school’s development of yearly theatre in education projects. These projects are developed in collaboration between the school and State of Play Arts, who work together to create an entirely bespoke and highly motivating theatre in education project, which utilises the Mantle of the Expert approach. These projects see the children going into role along with the actors, and carrying out their learning through a fictional frame, which will last for half a term. The actors will work with the children at the start of the project, before returning at a midpoint and then at the finale. In the intervening periods, the children stay in role, interacting with the storylines within their classrooms and taking the story in their own directions. When the actors return, they build upon the direction that the children have established, enabling the children to gain a sense that they are part of a ‘living story’ in which they are the key actors.
One such project was called ‘The Colour Thief’, in which the children were introduced to a fantasy world in which colours were disappearing (‘colours’ representing not only visual colours, but also the attributes that make us all unique). The children stepped into the story and joined the main characters on a quest to find out who the Colour Thief was. Following the first dramatic input by the actors, the children created maps of the fantasy world within their classrooms and decided upon the first steps they should take, engaging in creative writing and role play as they went on further adventures. When the actors came back in for the mid-point workshops, they built upon the children’s adventures so far, before introducing them to ‘The Colour Thief’, who it turned out had been stealing the colours on behalf of another mysterious character, who the children would now need to find. The children continued the adventure within the classroom, using their imaginations to search for the Colour Thief and inventing ways in which they could persuade the mysterious ‘Colour Thief’ to return the colours. The final workshop with the actors saw the children finally confront the real ‘Colour Thief’, taking part in a ‘philosophical battle’ to convince him that the colours should be restored.
As you can see, these projects have highly developed storylines, which are designed so that children can easily step into them, yet explore a range of complex themes and developments. Each project is designed to provide opportunities for children to explore a range of curriculum areas. One of the key outcomes of using this approach is that the children’s learning is highly purposeful and carried out for a clear reason. The projects also stimulate the child’s imaginative thinking, whilst also providing opportunities for high quality and motivating learning experiences within the classroom. The use of our Theatre in Education projects, in conjunction with our Mantle of the Expert approach, is an important way in which we seek to provide awe and wonder within our curriculum and develop enthusiastic and successful learners.
The school’s innovative work in developing these projects is documented in an article in ‘Drama – The National Drama Magazine of Professional Practice’.

Your Child’s Progress
During their time at Rushcombe First School, our aim is for every child to fulfil their potential across the full breadth of the curriculum, including key curriculum areas such as Mathematics, Reading and Writing. As a school, we also take a holistic view of your child’s development, recognising the importance of personal, social and emotional development within the context of the whole child.
Parent consultation evenings are organised on a termly basis for you to meet with your child’s class teacher to discuss their progress. These meetings provide an opportunity for parents to keep up to date with their child’s progress in school and to discuss next steps for learning.
At the end of each academic year, each child receives their annual report, which summarises the progress they have made during the year. For children in Years 1-4, progress is indicated against age related expectations for each National Curriculum subject area. Parents of children in Year 1 will also receive their child’s result from the national phonic screening test, whilst parents of children in Year 2 will receive details of their child’s SATS results. For children in Foundation, progress is indicated against each area from the Early Years Foundation Stage Profile.
In addition to the termly parent consultation meetings and your child’s annual report, we recognise that there may be other times during the year when you may need to meet with your child’s class teacher to discuss aspects of your child’s development. If this is the case, then please talk with your child’s class teacher to arrange a mutually convenient time.
